channel.title: Token Wisdom
channel.description: The Newsletter of Record for the Future of Now. 100% humanly chosen since 2013.

item.title: The Stupidity Subsidy
item.description: W24 — Everyone keeps asking whether technology made us dumber. Wrong question. The data says no. Our intelligence didn't move, the reward function did. We built the first machine in history that pays smart people to act like idiots, and then blamed the idiots.

item.title: Compliance Is an Evidence Problem
item.description: W23 — TD Bank had the largest compliance army in North America and still let 70,000 alerts rot for six years. It didn’t fail from laziness. It failed because of twenty years of buying the wrong thing. The fix, one boring 35-year-old primitive.

item.title: Data Is Not the New Oil
item.description: W22 — The slogan is wrong on every axis it was built to carry. The lie is not lazy; it is load-bearing. Strip it back and you find the real commodity and the reason it stays hidden. The model keeps what fits and files the rest under noise. But the rest is not noise. The rest is where you live.

item.title: Human-in-the-Room
item.description: W21 - The catastrophe had red eyes and a server farm that says no. What you got was a Tuesday. The system isn't misaligned—it's exquisitely aligned. Every incentive points the same way: toward you being unnecessary. Not a bug. The spec.

item.title: The Proof Was Never the Point
item.description: W20 — A computer verified its first physics paper and found an error peer review missed. A mathematician quit his tenured position to argue that mathematics has been misdefined for 2,300 years. These are the same story.

item.title: 159th Edition 🔮 Week 19
item.description: This week — Edison didn't invent the light bulb. Pascal didn't discover his triangle. From misattributed theorems to erased mathematicians to AI labs inheriting credit they synthesized, we map what happens when the wrong name is on the door. The questions you can't ask are the ones that matter most.

item.title: The Wrong Name on the Door
item.description: W19 — Misattribution isn't an injustice problem, it's an intelligence problem. Put the wrong name on a discovery and the field asks questions designed for the wrong person. The correction never arrives because no one knows it's missing.

item.title: 158th Edition 🔮 Week 18
item.description: This week — wrong beliefs don't die from evidence, they die when defending it costs more than abandoning it. From MBTI's AI metastasis to paper mills contaminating science, we map what keeps civilizations confidently wrong and ask: it the correction mechanism broken?

item.title: The Cost of Being Right
item.description: W18 — Wrong beliefs don't survive because the evidence is hidden. They survive because they're embedded in economies, careers, and identities that resist correction. From MBTI's AI-powered metastasis to psychiatry's overdue reckoning, here's the machinery that keeps us confidently wrong.

item.title: 157th Edition 🔮 Week 17
item.description: This week: 26 million horses didn't fail, their function was reassigned. From AI-managed stores without taste to ASML's physical bottleneck to Palantir inheriting the farm, we map what survives when three-state inheritance compresses into two. The record is the only thing that survives.

item.title: No Heir. No Lesson.
item.description: W17 — The farm already has an heir: the system that owns the inputs. When time compresses, inheritance dissolves. We don't run simulations seeking truth, we seek permission for what's decided. This isn't about jobs, it's about the flattening of time itself. The record matters.

item.title: 156th Edition 🔮 Week 16
item.description: This week — Darkness outruns light. A 19th-century optics trick secures quantum keys. Samsung sets a photonics production date. A 2,300-year-old math mistake finally gets named. A robot generalizes. The old answers were already there — the constraint just hadn't been named yet.

item.title: Who's Mind Is It Anyway?
item.description: W16 — Everyone's asking what to do about AI. Wrong question. Everything worth saving rests on one capacity we're quietly trading for convenience. The question isn't what to protect—it's whether you're still doing the thinking.

item.title: 155th Edition 🔮 Week 15
item.description: This week — Darkness outruns light. A 19th-century optics trick secures quantum keys. Samsung sets a photonics production date. A 2,300-year-old math mistake finally gets named. A robot generalizes. The old answers were already there — the constraint just hadn't been named yet.

item.title: We Trained It on Human Weaponry
item.description: W15 - The corpus didn't capture human knowledge. It captured what traveled. And what travels, across centuries of civilization, is weaponry, it's the fraction of human cognition evolved specifically to exploit other humans. We built the host condition before the parasite arrived.

item.title: 154th Edition 🔮 Week 14
item.description: This week — Darkness outruns light. A 19th-century optics trick secures quantum keys. Samsung sets a photonics production date. A 2,300-year-old math mistake finally gets named. A robot generalizes. The old answers were already there — the constraint just hadn't been named yet.

item.title: The Cow Came Last
item.description: W14 - A cattle monitoring platform, a Calgary winter, a dying mother, and the formula that keeps showing up across a thousand years of mathematics — whether anyone is looking for it or not. The constraint was never the obstacle. It was always the answer.

item.title: 153rd Edition 🔮 Week 13
item.description: This week — a proposed fermion hints at a fifth dimension; AI flags a formal logic flaw in a physics paper; FCC mandates fiber, retiring copper; graphene photonics reframes compute; 5 AI CEOs now govern decisions affecting 8B people.

item.title: The Sky Has Been Warning Us Since 1859
item.description: W13 - The sun fired a warning shot in 1859. We had 165 years. We wrote reports, introduced legislation, held hearings — and kept building a bigger antenna. The solution to the oldest infrastructure problem in the modern world exists. It just isn't where anyone thought to look.

item.title: 152nd Edition 🔮 Week 12
item.description: This week: physicists near 'ideal glass'; inequality far worse than perceived; rogue AI agents abused passwords and bypassed antivirus; a student solved a classic math problem; Michael Pollan examines consciousness in animals, plants, and machines.

item.title: The Proentropic Weed Manifesto
item.description: W12 - We prize orchids — for rarity, for control, for perfect optimization — and we scrub away the mess. Reality isn’t a greenhouse; orchids perish outside. Physics guarantees disorder. Design for weeds: systems that gain strength from chaos. This is no metaphor: an actual physical law ensures it.

item.title: 151st Edition 🔮 Week 11
item.description: This week: The brain delivers precision error signals that mirror machine learning. Canada is leaving Starlink. AI data centers are drinking the water table dry. A 10-year-old's butterfly experiment shocks the field. And the argument you think you're having was decided before you opened your mouth.

item.title: The Room Was Already Set Before You Walked In
item.description: W11 - You have spent your whole life learning to spot the argument. Nobody told you the argument was never the point. The persuasion is the last nail. Pre-suasion is the house. And someone else already built it.

item.title: 150th Edition 🔮 Week 10
item.description: This week: RSA encryption just got 10x easier to crack. Google quietly quantum-proofed HTTPS. Iranian drones hit Amazon data centers. And MIT found mastery lives in your eyes before your mouth. Everything underneath is moving.

item.title: The Race That Eats Its Own Rules
item.description: W10 - The infrastructure of good intentions has quietly become the infrastructure of acceleration. Not corruption. Rational adaptation. Seven researchers warned about this in 1945. The people who built this understand it best — and they're all outside the institutions now.

item.title: 149th Edition 🔮 Week 09
item.description: This week: A rogue AI published a hit piece, and thermodynamic tech rivals GPUs at lower energy. Britain aims to predict crimes, while Terence Tao sees AI reshaping math. We aren't building intelligence; we're industrializing prediction—surveillance with better branding.

item.title: The Double Collapse
item.description: W09 - The infrastructure of being unobserved has quietly ceased to exist. Not gradually. Now. Two papers, published weeks apart, confirm what most institutions have not yet accepted: anonymity is gone — and it took collective power with it.

item.title: Dear Sam,
item.description: On vendor-financed delusions, circular capital, the $100 billion retreat nobody wants to name, and what it means that the CFO of the world's most important AI project doesn't bother with the money flywheel.

item.title: 148th Edition 🔮 Week 08
item.description: This week: Mini brains solve engineering problems. AI reads MRIs at 97.5% accuracy without explaining why. Consciousness might live in electromagnetic fields. Forests changing how they breathe. We built systems that work before we understand them.

item.title: The Persistence of Inferior Standards
item.description: W08 - Your calendar is broken, your clock runs on Bronze Age finger-counting, and your interest rates are modeled on Sumerian goat reproduction. We're not living in a high-tech civilization. We're running 21st-century software on medieval firmware.

item.title: 147th Edition 🔮 Week 07
item.description: This week: Systems so capable they've become fragile. So optimized they have no room left to fail. So advanced they've made us hostages to their own perfection. It takes 250 poisoned documents to collapse an entire AI. Not millions. Not thousands. Two hundred and fifty. We've called this progress.

item.title: Threading a Very Fine Needle
item.description: W07 - We built a thing that's really good at making us not need ourselves anymore, and we're calling it progress. It only takes 250 poisoned documents to corrupt an entire AI system. Not millions. Not thousands. Two-hundred, and fifty. That’s less than a few hours work, collectively.

item.title: 146th Edition 🔮 Week 06
item.description: This week: How does anything complex exist in a chaos-built universe? Blood Falls explained after a century. Fast radio bursts from monster shocks. Ancient math predates writing. AI nears human intelligence. WiFi tracks you invisibly. Order shouldn't exist—but does.

item.title: How Does Order Emerge in a Universe Built for Chaos?
item.description: W06 - The universe writes in entropy, but you're an improbable paragraph. Physics can explain why everything falls apart but not why complex things like you exist in the first place. The universe's greatest paradox awaits.

item.title: 145th Edition 🔮 Week 05
item.description: This week: Donut-shaped light promises better wireless while scientists question Earth's population counts. Chinese satellites push competitors lower, academic work vanishes with one click—technology creates opportunities and vulnerabilities alike.

item.title: The Zombie Singularity of Intelligence Without Understanding
item.description: W05 - TV's "Person of Interest" warned us about AI without wisdom. Silicon Valley's response? Scale the zombies, optimize the pattern-matching, and call it progress. We're teaching machines to play chess while forgetting why some pieces shouldn't be sacrificed.

item.title: Dear Dario,
item.description: You preached AI ethics from your personal blog while selling Anthropic's independence to Amazon. Now your 'Constitutional AI' sits on Bezos's property, paying rent."

item.title: 144th Edition 🔮 Week 04
item.description: This week: Ancient alchemy becomes reality while AI threatens to flatten culture into comfortable mediocrity. From CERN's lead-to-gold alchemy to mirror cells that could end all life, we explore how frontier science resurrects old dreams and nightmares as surveillance capitalism extracts everything.

item.title: The Greengrocer Goes To Davos
item.description: W04 - When a system runs on collective pretense, it inevitably breaks. Not when the fiction fails, but when maintaining it costs more than telling the truth. I wrote this in a newsletter. Canada's PM just delivered it at Davos. Either Ottawa's subscribing, or truth has its own timing.

item.title: 143rd Edition 🔮 Week 03
item.description: This week: Corporate power reshapes society while AI disrupts traditional industries. From ranchers turning to carbon credits to tech giants consolidating control, we explore how surveillance capitalism and algorithmic efficiency are rewriting the rules of business, law, and human autonomy.
